claims.text: The proposed model will explicitly decouple lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-derived elastic constants and phonon dispersions will be used to calculate the lattice thermal conductivity.
An electronic-scattering framework beyond the standard Wiedemann–Franz law will independently predict electronic thermal conductivity.
The electronic-scattering framework will be calibrated using measured electrical resistivity.
The integrated model will predict thermal conductivity within ±15%.
The model will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 20–25% relative to earlier Debye-based analytical models.
Defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystals are the applicable sample state for the low-temperature lattice calculation and validation.
HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen are the applicable sample state for high-temperature total-conductivity validation.
Below 200 K, experiments will primarily probe lattice thermal conductivity in near-perfect HfNbTaTiZr crystals.
Measurements from 300 to 1200 K on specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen provide total thermal-conductivity data.
Electron-electron interactions, Fermi smearing, and Fermi-surface effects can cause departures from the standard Wiedemann–Franz approximation.
Using explicit phonon dispersions rather than a single Debye temperature will accurately capture phonon dynamics.
Accounting for non-ideal electron interactions will overcome limitations of Wiedemann–Franz-based electronic-conductivity estimates.
The model will reproduce low-temperature lattice thermal conductivity within ±15%.
The model will reproduce the upward trend in total thermal conductivity from 300 to 1200 K within ±15%.
Previous approaches largely relied on simplified Debye-temperature approximations.
Previous approaches conflated lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions.
The model's validity is limited to defect-free low-temperature samples and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing high-temperature samples and may fail with additional uncontrolled defects.

The hypothesis is falsified if either lattice or total conductivity differs from prediction by more than ±15%, or if independent electronic measurements cannot be reconciled with the predicted electronic contribution.
